title: Language core: collections internals and type hints (Python)
seriesDescription: dict, list, set, deque internals, generics and typing, mypy. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Python list, dict, set and deque internals and costs, aliasing and mutation-while-iterating traps, heapq, Counter, and type hints with TypeVar and generics.
source: Python docs: data structures, collections, heapq, typing; the CPython dict implementation notes; Real Python; Fluent Python (Ramalho); GeeksforGeeks and Toptal Python interview lists

questions.prompt: In Python 3.7 and later, a dict iterates its keys in insertion order as part of the language guarantee.

options.why: Correct: this became a language guarantee in 3.7 (an implementation detail of CPython 3.6).
It is guaranteed, not just a CPython quirk; collections.OrderedDict only adds extras like move_to_end and order-sensitive equality.

questions.explanation: CPython keeps a compact entries array plus a sparse index table. Mutating a dict while iterating it raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about CPython dictionaries.
questions.text: CPython implements a dict as a {1} table that resolves collisions with {2} addressing (probing), so a lookup is {3} on average.
questions.explanation: A CPython dict does not chain colliding entries in buckets; it probes other slots of one flat table, which keeps lookups O(1) on average while the table stays sparse.

questions.prompt: Match each Python structure to its defining property.

right.text: Dynamic array: O(1) indexing and amortised append, O(n) insert at the front
Doubly linked blocks: O(1) append and popleft at both ends
Hash table of key-value pairs that iterates in insertion order
Hash table of unique hashable items with O(1) average membership tests
Binary min-heap stored in a list: heappop is O(log n)
Balanced tree with keys always sorted

questions.explanation: Choose by access pattern: index (list), both ends (deque), lookup by key (dict), membership (set), smallest-first (heapq).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: collections.deque.popleft() takes O(1) time, whereas list.pop(0) takes O(n).
questions.reason: A Python list is implemented as a doubly linked list of nodes.

whys.a: R is false: a list is a dynamic array of pointers.
whys.b: R is false, so option b cannot hold.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the list shifts every remaining pointer); R is false because CPython lists are arrays of pointers (that is why index access is O(1)).
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Use deque for queues (BFS); a list is fine for stacks (append/pop at the end).

questions.prompt: How many elements does len({1, 1.0, True, "1", (1,)}) return? Note that 1 == 1.0 == True in Python.
questions.explanation: 1, 1.0 and True are equal and hash equally, so they collapse to one element; "1" and (1,) are distinct. That leaves 3.

questions.prompt: Write Python that removes all even numbers from the list nums in place (the same list object must end up with only the odd numbers) without skipping elements.
questions.model: nums[:] = [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0]
questions.explanation: Assigning to the slice nums[:] replaces the contents in place. Looping and calling remove() while iterating skips elements, so iterate over a copy or rebuild.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

l = [1, 2, 2, 3]
for v in l:
    if v == 2:
        l.remove(v)
print(l)

What is the output?

options.why: Correct: removing shifts later items left while the iterator index moves on, so one 2 is never visited.

options.text: [1, 3], since both 2s are removed by the loop
options.why: That would need the loop to see both 2s, but the shift makes it skip one.

options.text: RuntimeError: list changed size while looping
options.why: Only dicts and sets raise that error; a list silently misbehaves.

options.text: [1, 2, 2, 3], because remove inside a loop has no effect
options.why: remove does modify the list; it just does it unpredictably here.

questions.explanation: Never mutate a list while looping over it; build a new list or iterate over a copy.

options.text: RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration
options.why: Correct: adding a key while iterating invalidates the iterator, and the dict detects it.

options.text: It loops forever as new keys keep being added
options.why: The dict raises an error on the next step instead of looping.

options.text: d ends as {1: "a", 11: "b"} with no error
options.why: The size check makes the loop fail before it can finish quietly.
Assigning a new key is allowed; the failure comes from the iteration.

questions.explanation: Iterate over list(d) or d.copy() if you need to change the dict inside the loop.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

grid = [[0] * 3] * 3
grid[0][0] = 1
print(grid)

What is the output?

options.why: Correct: the outer * 3 repeats a reference to one inner list, so all three rows are the same object.
Wrong: this is what you would get from [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)], which builds three separate rows.
Wrong: only index 0 of the shared row is assigned, so the other columns stay 0.

options.text: TypeError: list assignment is not allowed here
options.why: Wrong: lists are mutable and item assignment on a nested list is perfectly legal.

questions.explanation: Sequence repetition copies references, not objects. Use a comprehension to create independent rows. Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: Write Python that builds a dict counts mapping each word in the list words to how many times it appears.

checks.label: loops or uses a counter class

questions.model:
from collections import Counter
counts = Counter(words)
questions.explanation: Counter is the idiomatic answer; a dict with get(w, 0) + 1, or defaultdict(int), is equally good.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function first(items) with type hints using a TypeVar named T so that mypy infers the element type of the sequence it returns.

checks.label: parameter is a Sequence/list of T

questions.explanation: On Python 3.12+ you can write def first[T](items: Sequence[T]) -> T. Type hints are not enforced at runtime; mypy or pyright check them statically.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Testing membership with in is faster on a set than on a list when the collection is large.
questions.reason: A set stores its items in a hash table, so membership is O(1) on average, whereas a list scans up to n items.

whys.a: Correct: the hash-table lookup is exactly why the set is faster than a linear scan.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: the hash-table lookup is exactly why the set is faster than a linear scan.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: the hash-table lookup is exactly why the set is faster than a linear scan.
whys.d: This option says A is false and R is true, which does not match: the hash-table lookup is exactly why the set is faster than a linear scan.

questions.explanation: Convert a list to a set first when you run many membership tests.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Python dict keeps its keys in insertion order.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: Both statements are true, but hashability is unrelated to why order is preserved (a compact entries array records insertion order).
whys.b: Correct: Both statements are true, but hashability is unrelated to why order is preserved (a compact entries array records insertion order).
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: Both statements are true, but hashability is unrelated to why order is preserved (a compact entries array records insertion order).
whys.d: This option says A is false and R is true, which does not match: Both statements are true, but hashability is unrelated to why order is preserved (a compact entries array records insertion order).

questions.explanation: Order preservation is a language guarantee since Python 3.7; hashability is what makes O(1) lookup possible.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Python enforces type hints at run time by raising an error when an argument has the wrong type.
questions.reason: Annotations are stored on the function in its __annotations__ attribute.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: A is false: the interpreter ignores hints when calling; R is true, which is how tools and libraries read them.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: A is false: the interpreter ignores hints when calling; R is true, which is how tools and libraries read them.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: A is false: the interpreter ignores hints when calling; R is true, which is how tools and libraries read them.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: the interpreter ignores hints when calling; R is true, which is how tools and libraries read them.

questions.explanation: Hints are checked by external tools such as mypy, or by libraries that choose to read __annotations__.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about Python containers.

options.why: The list over-allocates, so most appends write into spare capacity.

options.text: A dict key must be hashable.
options.why: The key is hashed to find its slot, so it needs a stable hash.
Every existing element shifts one place to the right.

options.text: A set preserves insertion order like a dict.
A tuple is a hashable key even if it holds a list.
options.why: Hashing a tuple hashes its items, and a list is unhashable.

questions.explanation: Know the costs: append is cheap, insertion at the front is linear, hashing requires immutability.
